name: whole-part
intent: Aggregate several collaborating components into one semantic unit whose Whole encapsulates its Parts, organises their collaboration and owns their creation and destruction, so that clients use a single interface and the part-of lifetime holds by construction.
problem: A composite object must be assembled from parts that have no valid life of their own: each part carries state and resources of its own, yet the aggregation's invariants (totals, ordering, referential integrity, exclusive use) hold only while every part is present and untouchable from outside. Without a single owner, callers create parts in the wrong order, keep handles to parts that the owning object has already replaced or destroyed, share one part between two aggregates, and leak whatever nobody agreed to release.
context: Aggregate and containment structures inside one component or module - an order and its lines, a document and its paragraphs, a pool and its connections, a scene graph and its nodes, a composite entity and its children - where the parts are not shared with other aggregates, where the whole enforces invariants over them, and where the lifetime of the parts must be sequenced (parts created before the whole is usable, released after it stops being usable). The pattern is recursive: a whole can itself be a part of a larger whole, so the same ownership rules apply at every level of the object graph.
benefits: Lifecycle ownership is centralised: the whole creates, keeps and destroys its parts, so parts cannot be orphaned, doubly owned or silently forgotten by callers.
Invariants over the parts (sums, ordering, uniqueness, referential integrity, resource accounting) are enforced at one boundary instead of being re-checked by every client.
Clients depend on a single interface; the internal decomposition - even the existence of individual parts - can change without touching call sites.
Exclusive ownership removes aliasing: no part is reachable from two wholes, so there is exactly one place that mutates it and one place that releases it.
Recursive composition lets the same containment rules and the same operations apply uniformly at every level of a hierarchy instead of special-casing leaves.
Construction and destruction must be written together, which surfaces partial-construction failures instead of hiding them behind half-built aggregates.
tradeoffs: The whole easily becomes a god object and a bottleneck: containment tempts you to route every operation on every part through the common interface.
Exclusive ownership forbids sharing, so genuinely shared data must be duplicated (memory plus consistency cost) or moved out of the pattern into a flyweight, lookup or reference-based structure.
Concurrent work on different parts is serialised through the owner, and the whole's lock, borrow or monitor becomes the contention point of the aggregation.

Destruction order and partial construction are the subtle failure paths: a constructor that fails halfway must release the parts it already created, and reverse-order destruction has to respect dependencies between parts.
In garbage-collected languages nothing forces the whole's cleanup to run at all: without an explicit close/dispose path the pattern degrades into a leak of file handles, connections and locks.
Direct part access is gone by design, so traversal-heavy or bulk algorithms need read-only views, iterators or projections that the whole must deliberately publish.

participants.responsibility: Encapsulates its parts, owns their lifecycle (creation, replacement, destruction), enforces the aggregation's invariants and publishes the only client-visible interface to the functionality the parts implement.

Constituent component with no independent lifecycle: it exists only as part of its whole, may reach its whole for context through a non-owning back-reference, and is never handed out as a mutable handle.
Uses the whole's interface only; never creates, destroys or reaches into parts directly, and sees part state through the views, copies or queries the whole deliberately exposes.

use_cases: Aggregate roots in a domain model: an order owns its lines and is the only handle the application, the repository and the UI pass around; adding, replacing and deleting a line happens through the order.

Resource-owning components: a connection pool owns the connections it created and its accounting; closing the pool releases every connection, and no code outside the pool holds a live connection object.
Document and editor models: a document owns paragraphs, styles and embedded objects, enforces cross-references between them, and offers the operations the UI binds to.
Scene graphs and simulation hierarchies: a node owns its children and their local transforms, so traversal, update and teardown are recursive operations of the owning tree.

Persistence aggregates with framework-enforced lifecycle: a JPA/Hibernate parent entity mapped @OneToMany(cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true) owns its children's persistence - deleting the parent cascades the deletes, and a child removed from the parent's collection is automatically deleted; only the parent's add/remove helper methods keep both sides of the ownership link in sync.
Compiler and query trees: a root owns its nodes and hands out read-only views or visitors, so a node can never be spliced into another tree or mutated behind the root's back.

Language-enforced whole-part: a Rust struct owns its fields - when a value goes out of scope its Drop::drop runs and drop glue then recursively drops the owned fields, and after a partially successful construction only the initialised fields are dropped, so the language guarantees the whole releases exactly the parts it created.
avoid_when: The components have independent lifecycles - shared between aggregates, attached and detached at runtime, or referenced from elsewhere: use explicit references (or a flyweight/lookup) instead of pretending containment.
A single immutable value with no sub-objects is sufficient: model it as a value object; wrapping it in an owning whole adds indirection without adding an invariant.
The parts are interchangeable policies chosen at runtime: Strategy or plain delegation composes an interface, and the whole has no reason to own the implementation.
The goal is a uniform interface over heterogeneous nodes with client-supplied recursion: Composite is the closer pattern - it optimises uniformity of treatment, and ownership is incidental to it.
The aggregate is a transport or serialisation structure that is copied between layers: a record/DTO with value semantics is simpler, and ownership semantics only get in the way.
A framework already gives the aggregation its lifetime (ORM-managed entity clusters, DI-scoped components, UI element trees): let the container own the parts instead of rebuilding the hierarchy.
anti_patterns: Leaky aggregation: accessors that return the live part collection or mutable part objects, so clients mutate parts behind the whole's back and every invariant becomes unenforceable.
God whole: every operation on every part is funnelled through the common interface until the whole is a facade over the entire subsystem rather than one semantic unit.

Exclusive ownership simulated with shared references (singletons, registries, sibling pointers between parts): ownership turns ambiguous and destruction degenerates into double release, dangling handles or leaks.
Whole without destruction: the whole creates parts that hold file handles, connections or locks and never releases them, which is a resource leak dressed up as encapsulation.
Shallow sharing of a whole: copying the whole (or serialising and rehydrating it) while the parts stay referenced elsewhere, so two 'owners' mutate one part.
Containment imposed on data that is genuinely shared: duplicating the parts to keep the ownership fiction, which trades a design problem for a consistency bug.
design_principles: Encapsulation and information hiding: parts are private state; the whole is the only published surface of the aggregation.
Single responsibility per role: exactly one owner per resource, so creation and destruction stay symmetric and auditable.
Composition over inheritance: the aggregation is built from parts, not by widening a base class.
Invariants at the boundary: validate in the whole's operations so clients can never observe a half-formed or inconsistent aggregation.
Least privilege for parts: a part that must know its whole gets a non-owning back-reference, never a strong one that would let it extend the whole's lifetime.
best_practices: Create parts inside the whole's constructor or factory and release them in its destructor/close; keep construction and destruction mirror images of each other.
Never publish mutable part handles: return read-only views, copies or domain-level queries instead.
Make the whole the consistency boundary: check invariants before a mutation commits and keep multi-part updates atomic.
Design for partial-construction failure: whichever part creation fails, release everything already created (RAII, try-with-resources, scope guards).
Keep the whole's interface at the level of domain operations (addLine, total, renameParagraph) instead of part plumbing (setLineName, getLineList).
Prefer exclusive ownership; when a part must be shared, model the sharing explicitly and make any part-to-whole link weak so parts never keep their whole alive.
Express ownership in the types where the language allows it: smart pointers, move-only types, unexported fields, read-only collections and borrowed parameters are the cheapest enforcement available.
sources: Buschmann, Meunier, Rohnert, Sommerlad & Stal, Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture, Volume 1: A System of Patterns (1996) - Chapter 3 'Design Patterns', Whole-Part, p. 225 (category Structural Decomposition).
Halper, Geller et al., An OODB part-whole model, Data & Knowledge Engineering 27 (1998) 59-95 - https://web.njit.edu/~geller/PersonalPublicationArchive.1/An%20OODB%20Part-Whole_Oct1997.pdf
